Arkanaut features, as you might imagine, a company of Arkanauts – a pioneering and entrepreneurial crew of Kharadron Overlords. This rugged band are led by the enterprising Captain Orra, accompanied by the grizzled navigator Frodrikk.

The other big feature of the show, and almost a character in its own right, is the ship itself.

The Therodoson

Many Arkanaut ships are made to standard patterns, but are subsequently improved upon by their crew, who treat the vessel as ship, home, transport, castle, and fire support. Frigates, even more so than the Gunhaulers of the Grundstok and the Ironclad flagships, are as diverse as the privateer Kharadron that call them home.

The Therodoson is a particularly fine example. Hailing from the port of Barak-Zilfin, a city renowned for the speed of its ships and the daring of its sailors, this once-proud ship, like its crew, has fallen on hard times, and is long overdue for a trip to the Endrin Dock.

There are a few things a long-bearded Kharadron fan might notice about the Therodoson.

The runic inscription on the hull of the skyvessel is unique to every ship. Kharadron runes trace their lineage to the ancient Khazalid empire. In this instance the runes on the side of the Therodoson read “fearless seeker of fate and fortune”.

The Therodoson also sports a heavy skyhook, and unlike the Frigate miniature, which has an enclosed gunner’s canopy, the Therodoson has a partly open hatch (similar to that on the Ironclad miniature). This sort of modification is typical of the kind of customisation an Arkanaut crew might make to their vessel.

Because of the nature of animation, we get to see some parts of the Frigate in more detail than even the original Citadel miniature. We particularly enjoyed the detailing around the helm. True to the miniature, but necessarily more detailed, it features wheels, dials, levers, and the critical aether-gold gauge.

Da Red Gobbo is back with another festive miniature – and this time he’s got himself a Squigmobile. Just make sure you’re out of the way – we’re not convinced he knows how to stop!

Da Red Gobbo’s Squigmobile is a roaring, clanking contraption geared towards delivering presents at exceptionally high speed, which we dare say channels more than a few Wazdakka Gutsmek vibes. His long-suffering ‘elf’ assistant looks frankly miserable in the bomb-shaped sidecar – which honestly might just be a live bomb – but knowing what a jolly fellow Da Red Gobbo can be, he’s probably overreacting.

See, da Gobbo is a safety-conscious boss. He’s even wearing a helmet.*

This miniature will be available to pre-order soon, and if you want to use it in some fun casual games, make sure to grab this year’s Festive Activities Guide from your local Warhammer store in November. It contains Legends rules for Warhammer 40,000, Nemesis Operatives rules for Kill Team, and as unlikely as it sounds, Blood Bowl rules.

Alongside the Squigmobile, our favourite yuletide revolutionary stars in a brand-new novella from Chem Dog author Callum Davis – Da Red Gobbo’s Reckoning.

This raucous tale revolves around the ratling fixer Ector Flynn and his squad of snipers, who are sent into a snow-cloaked wasteland by choleric Catachan commanders to hunt Da Red Gobbo down. After months of being bullied and knocked around by the Jungle Fighters, Flynn’s team welcome the chance to finally prove their worth, but nothing goes to plan when Da Gobbo is involved and they may come back learning a little something about vengeance from their red-coated quarry.

Keep an eye on Warhammer Community to find out when you can pick up the new miniature and book. In the meantime, catch up with the rest of Da Red Gobbo’s adventures with Long Live Da Red Gobbo, Da Gobbo’s Demise, Da Gobbo’s Revenge, and Da Gobbo Rides again – all available via the Black Library app.

She crouched to listen to the stones, and through their vibrations, the stones spoke back.

‘The troggoths are in the western gallery, Thrynn,’ Helgur said, standing and brushing herself down. Over her head soared an archway of immaculate stone: the boundary mark of Karak Vigg. Beyond that was the tunnel ceiling, glimmering faintly, arcing down towards the half-finished gate into the hold behind them. ‘On the move now, as you might imagine.’

‘How long until they reach us?’ Thrynn Bjarki was a mountain of cave-bear fur, polished gromril and the accoutrements of various clans and guilds – a figure carved, as if by the Maker himself, into a monument to Khazalite culture. Amidst it all was a face and eyes that were stern but not quite unkind. Helgur shrugged, remaining just on the right side of respectful, as she dusted off her hands and glanced along the gloom-gripped passage before them.

‘With the luck of the Whitebeard? Still not long. Especially if the alpha-beast is among them. Likely before Kyng Vargrimm and his reinforcements arrive.’

‘Time enough to burn out any last nerves with a drink, though.’ The interjection was vigorous, lit with an undercurrent of flame. Helgur and Bjarki turned and watched as a wildly mohicaned warrior clad in drake pelt and gold approached from the duardin throng gathered at the hold’s entrance behind them.

Considering she had scowled through every war council and Great Recitation, Volna grinned now. It was an unusual expression on the scarred face of Urgma-Grimnir’s daughter; then again, it was unusual on the face of any Fyreslayer. Volna wore her battle-lust openly, though, three tankards of frothing magmalt ale drawn from the kegs the duardin had brought with them clutched in her broad hands.

‘One for you too, our worthy Stonesmith.’ The Fyreslayer thrust the sloshing mug at Helgur, downing a great swill of ale and wiping her mouth on the back of her hand.

‘I’m no Stonesmith, Runedaughter.’ Helgur took a drink, but her voice was terse. ‘I’m no less a fighter than you, as were all my line. I just… hear the stones.’

‘I hear them too, lass. You know what they tell me?’ Volna’s cinderous eyes flashed. ‘They talk of death. They talk about righting one more wrong. They talk of opening throats and splitting bellies and cleansing the rock with trogg blood. You know about that, lass? You know about vengeance?’

‘Aye,’ Helgur spat, reaching to the pendant around her neck. Her father’s sharp rune-work bumped beneath her finger, as it had many times since she had recovered it from what remained of his pulverised body. ‘Aye, I know about that.’

‘Enough, both of you. Defending the karak is what matters.’ Bjarki downed his own ale and gestured with his hammer back along the tunnel, to where pillars and half-built arches marked the edge of the Khazalites’ reconstruction efforts. ‘Grimnir would have our wrath saved for our enemies.’

‘See to your own duties, Thrynn. We’ll mind the Burning Berserker’s legacy.’ A harsh, gruff laugh left Volna as she raised her tankard in acknowledgement. A breath later and she turned, scale-cloak swirling, to march back to her glowering kin and grunting droth-beast at the eastern edge of the throng.

‘Strange folk, those Grimmdron slayers,’ Helgur said once she was gone, head shaking.

‘They might say the same of you, given how easily they bait you,’ Bjarki said, hammer braced over a shoulder. ‘I know you’re eager, lass. Just don’t lose sight of what we’re fighting for.’ 

‘Remembrance is strength. Through honouring what has been, we craft what is yet to be.’

‘Quoting my own words back at me, eh?’ Bjarki chuckled. He shook his head, beard swaying and clan-totems clinking. ‘Ah, niece. Your father was the same when we were lads, but he learned wisdom. We don’t put such stock in remembrance just to kindle hate. We remember to remind ourselves what is at stake.’ 

‘I know, lord-uncle,’ Helgur grunted, head bowed but not quite chastised. ‘But since it was this sort of beast that took him from us, some grudgement might be excused.’

‘Grudgement, aye. But grudgement must serve a purpose. Left untended, it digs to unhappy delves,’ Bjarki said, his tone suddenly severe. It did not last long before he sighed and clapped Helgur on the shoulder. 

‘Go on, girl. Greet your mother for me should you see her.’

Helgur set off at a steady jog, braids jostling. She passed ranks of duardin preparing for battle, acknowledging some with nods or grunts. Clans of axe and hammer compared the craftsmanship of their weapons; gunners sat carving resonant glyphs upon their ammunition; Runewrights performed final checks on the arcane mechanisms of great Oathkeeper guns. 

Amongst the war throng stood the Gholems. Each warrior-monolith seemed to possess its own gravity. The Gazulite Gholems, clutching their two-handed hammers, stood apart, the duardin who huddled around them chanting in low, morbid tones. Passing them, Helgur headed for the gleam of gold banding that marked the Valayan Gholems and the shield-maids clustered around them. 

‘How was your uncle?’ It was still odd, seeing Imnod clad as a templar of the hearth-goddess. That said, Helgur had always thought her mother had a severe aspect, and the tight mail coif and ceremonial hair buns had not diminished that impression. Perhaps that was why the matrons of Valaya’s guardian-shrine had recruited her. The will of the ancestors, they had said. That the summons came hours before they were due to have laid Helgur’s father to rest could not be helped.

‘Resolute, mother,’ Helgur said. ‘I expected more…’

‘Fire?’ Imnod asked, eyebrow arched. ‘Every battle is an echo of another. Through those echoes, we recall the virtue of those who fought them, so we might honour them.’

‘Words of the hearth-guardian?’

‘Of my own, girl!’ Imnod’s laughter was brief. Soon her face grew firm, and she gestured back along the torch-lit underway. ‘Beyond this gate lie our forges, our hearths, our folk. Now these beasts come to reduce all that to rubble. Steel and courage will cast them back.’

‘So folk keep telling me,’ Helgur nodded. ‘But I would rather honour Thorgrim and keep my grudge burning hot.’

A deep, bass gurgling echoed from further down the passage. As a hush fell over the throng, there came a wave of stench. Warriors jostled into position, shields locking. Imnod disappeared back into the ranks of her closed order. Helgur took position in the back ranks of her own warrior band just in time for someone to raise the cry.

‘Troggoths!’

The host of horribles shambled from the gloom, knuckles dragging and mauls carving furrows. They were accelerating. From amongst the Khazalite lines, light flashed and arcane energy left its peculiar odour as cannon-tenders struck the runes of activation, seeing their machines belch obliterating shot. Gunners joined the salvo, bullets whistling into eyes and soft flesh. Volna’s blazing slayers were already in motion; the right flank of the throng had charged to smash into the troggoth mob’s own, incinerating beast-flesh as they went. And all the while, the rest of the warrior throng clanged weapons against shields like great echoing gongs, stomped their feet and began to chant.

‘Clan Valankrom, who burned the gruel-beasts from the pits of Angaraz and made Ayadah safe anew, we remember your courage!’

‘The clans of Hasgaard, who honoured Grimnir and stood firm against the hordes of the Troggoth King, we remember your ferocity!’

‘Valaya the Defender, who broke the Gargant’s Gate and saved the clans of Karak Mogram, we remember your fortitude!’

‘And we remember those murdered by beasts,’ Helgur murmured quietly, reaching up to her father’s charm, ‘in whose name I will slay a hundred.’

Many troggoths had been engaged by the Fyreslayers; as sparks flew from gold-inlaid weapons, Helgur saw Volna’s Magmadroth rear up and let loose a blazing flame-stream at the mammoth brute grappling with it. But the rest of the beasts remained a juddering avalanche, and now they hit home. The first rank of duardin were knocked sprawling by their momentum. Not so the second. At Bjarki’s bellowed insistence, they gritted teeth, dug in heels, bent backs and pushed. They strode back against the troggoths even as the dull beasts grunted, baffled at why these little things were not simply breaking. They cleaved bellies or pinned beasts in place as firepower ripped through them. 

Imnod’s henge of Valayans was with them, drawing the enemy’s rage onto themselves while their long halberds speared and sliced. Helgur, along with the other reserve warriors, was preparing to join the scrum when an unhealthy groaning echoed off the tunnel wall beside them. In that pain was a warning, one that raked along Helgur’s spine.

‘The alpha-beast,’ she whispered as she fruitlessly scanned the fighting. ‘Inghilde’s lantern, where’s the alpha?’ 

There was an explosion of stone, a rush of force. Helgur was knocked from her feet as masonry and rock spun; it was this that saved her, her kin instead pulped into smears. As she blinked through the grit-haze, the sight of something monstrous shouldering through the destruction saw her spit a curse. The troggoth chief’s body seethed with motion: scuttling creatures of the deep and dark. In each hand, it carried half of an immense ancestor statue ground down into a club. 

Helgur doubted it had meant to punch through as part of some coordinated flank attack. Likely it had just wandered into a different tunnel and heard the sound of their chanting on the other side of the wall. Those beady yellow eyes locked upon her. She reached for her father’s charm, hoping to draw some measure of fury from it. Her fingers found the rune etched there. It was then, only then, that she recognised the pattern.

In her grief, in her grudgement, Helgur had not looked too closely at the actual design. She had presumed it was a weapon-rune. It was not; it was galaz. ‘Precious’. 

The beast looked along the duardin passageway, drawn towards the reclaimed works of the Khazalites by the light. Few save Helgur stood in its path of demolition. And, to her own surprise, that realisation burned through thoughts of vengeance.

‘I remember you, father,’ Helgur whispered. ‘I remember what you died for. Remember me as I die for it too.’

Getting to her feet, she moved to charge. The troggoth bellowed, raising a makeshift bludgeon. It swung, and her world went black – because she had closed her eyes. But the eternal darkness that should have followed did not. Instead came the resonant clang of weapon against shield. 

The orestone at the heart of each of the Valayan Gholems glowed with pulsing blue light as they stomped between Helgur and the marauding titan. Furious at being denied an easy meal, the troggoth set its shoulders and barged into them. One toppled, still swinging as it fell. The rest stood firm as the deep and resonant songs of Imnod’s henge of warriors flowed over the melee. The Gholems bashed the beast with their shields, splitting its lumpen nose. One hacked off an ear before having its own head annihilated with a wild swing.

A spinning shard of stone cut open Helgur’s cheek, seeing her flinch. The Gholems, for all their heroism, were being broken open. But they had bought seconds – crucial, unbending seconds. Seconds enough for a horn-blast to ring and the torches back down the underway passage to glow bright. Feet stamped and shields clanged to the echo of chanting, this time with force enough to shake the mountain.

Even as the Gholems battered it, the troggoth turned, brow furrowed – just as a spear of hexagonal rock burst from the earth and punched through its gut like an ore-pressing piston. The beast howled, dazed, as something equally huge sailed along an undulating current of rock towards it. Surrounded now by the Gholems, Helgur joined the cheers as the throne-barge of Kyng Vargrimm crashed forth, the duardin lord slicing through the troggoth’s neck with one punishing axe-swing. 

Warriors parted before him as the Kyng rode into the fray, the broken stone left by the troggoth’s entrance curving like a tube-wave at the chanting of Vargrimm’s Stonesmiths. Lightning spat from the drake-headed prows of his vessel, adding their firepower to the roaring barrage the Oathkeepers fired in his honour. Fresh clan warriors marched behind him, banners flashing with the sigils of the hold. Even some of Volna’s kin came with them, magmic veins of power threading along muscles as they sang ur-songs of awakening and doom.

Whatever intellect the troggoths possessed was not enough to see them retreat in time. Little by little, the duardin spilled over them, and their weapon arms did not tire. Helgur saw Imnod atop a felled brute, expression unbending as she stabbed down into its gaping mouth while shielding a wounded clan warrior with her body. Panicked, heavy breaths finally escaped Helgur’s chest. She allowed herself to sit as her heart slowed its hammering. One hand still clutched her amulet. 

‘I did not slay a single one, father. Not a single one.’ As she spoke, Helgur felt herself smile. Her body slumped against the leg of a Gholem, the stone warrior having now returned to a motionless docility. She glanced back along the underway. The torches burned bright. The pillars remained uncracked. The artifice of the duardin was unmarred. And where there was artifice, there was life. That, at least, was what the stones said to her now.

‘But I remembered. Remembered that vengeance isn’t everything. That we’re here to build, not just to slay. Perhaps that’s a good start, aye?’

The new Khazalite Holds Clanshields kit is packed with awesome build options, making it simple to customise your unit. Take a look at just how many ways you can put together the miniatures.

The 10 miniatures come with interchangeable shields – 10 with one rune so you can have a unified look, and the other 10 with different runes to mix it up.

The heads are also interchangeable and there are enough with beards that you can give them all a hirsute appearance if you like. 

Each Clanshield can be armed with a hammer or an axe – they have the same in-game profile as each other, and if the Kromdron can’t pick a favourite then you shouldn’t have to either.

The kit also includes parts to build an optional champion, standard bearer, and musician, all with more cosmetic options. The champion has a choice of two tactical rocks and three icon plates that they share with the standard bearer. Speaking of your banner waver, they have a choice of two standards, each with a choice of toppers, while the musician can choose from two different warhorns.

As well as being an incredibly flexible kit, the Clanshields are the backbone of Khazalite Holds armies. Their 3+ save makes them resilient and they get to add 1 to their wound rolls when they have any grudge marks.

At each Grand Narrative event, influential and charismatic characters known as the Lords of War command each of the player factions and use the support of their followers to achieve their goals, be it the salvation of an Imperial world or the summoning of a great daemon.

Let’s find out who our intrepid commanders will be fighting for this year as we head to Ferrum’s Wake.

Kaelen Voss, the Free Captain

Kaelen Voss first knew freedom in the moment he abandoned duty and death amidst the ranks of the Executioners Chapter to follow Huron Blackheart. He embraced the Tyrant of Badab not out of love for the Dark Gods, but because rebellion opened his eyes to a cold, inescapable truth. The Corpse-Emperor’s Imperium gifted him genetically enhanced might, eidetic memory, limitless brilliance, and an artificially long life with which to enjoy it, yet demanded inevitable death amidst eternal war as payment. Its oaths had bound him. In Huron’s revolt, Kaelen believed he had found the freedom to choose his own fate.

He was not alone in that belief. Many Red Corsairs sustained their treachery with simple vices: vengeance, ambition, blood, plunder, survival. Kaelen chose philosophy. He spoke of the lie of service, the corruption of thrones, the slow murder of duty, and the cowardice of men who named obedience virtue because they feared the void beyond it. Amidst an unapologetically traitorous band, Kaelen saw himself as a bastion of nobility.

Then Huron’s rebellion became a kingdom. It acquired rites, hierarchies, sorcerers, daemonic bargains, whispered devotions, and all the old shapes of servitude wearing the new, vibrant colours of the Maelstrom. Kaelen watched warriors who had spat on the Imperial Creed bow their heads to warp-born things. He saw free captains become courtiers. He saw rebellion harden into another chain.

So he rebelled again.

Renaming his strike cruiser Unbound Horizon, with a core of his oldest battle-brothers in tow, Kaelen abandoned service to Huron and escaped the Maelstrom. Drift, design, or damnation took him to the world of Ferrum’s Wake, where philosophy became proselytisation. Naming himself liberator, he shattered command spires, cut noospheric networks, armed underhive districts, and broadcast a promise through every vox-channel on the planet: no gods, no masters, no chains.

The people of Ferrum’s Wake believed him, and expressed that belief through the song of civil war.

In the aftermath of its liberation, billions sing Kaelen’s name as that of a conqueror. They offer him tithe and worship in equal measure, begging him to ascend to mastery of their world. At every turn, the Free Captain denies their offerings. His only demand is absolute devotion to liberty, no matter the cost or chaos it incurs.

As the Maelstrom swells bright in the void, Kaelen Voss’ fervent commitment to freedom only strengthens. He prepares the world, its fleets, and all those who share his cause for the inevitable vengeance to come. He will not kneel to the Emperor. He will not bend to Huron. He will not bargain with the gods. Upon Ferrum’s Wake, the Free Captain will make his stand.

The Warrant

The thing called The Warrant sits upon a brazen throne on a benighted warship. Commanding a fleet of heretics, renegades, oath-breakers, and blood-mad supplicants, it approaches Ferrum’s Wake with undeniable purpose.

The Warrant approaches Ferrum’s Wake for the head of Kaelen Voss.

It claims to be Huron Blackheart’s punishment wrought in adamantine and iron-hard muscle: an executioner and warlord whose existence is less a state of being, more a passage of judgment. Among the Red Corsairs, deserters whisper of it in sealed compartments and dying vox-bursts. They say no writ is needed where The Warrant walks. None have ever seen the Tyrant of Badab acknowledge the creature, much less command it, but who would dare doubt its provenance beneath the shadow of an axe?

Its armour bears old Corsair markings beneath layers of ritual scoring, brass kill-runes, and tally marks cut too deep to be mere decoration. Its helm is smooth where a face should declare identity. Whether the Warrant was once a failed Red Corsairs aspirant, some daemon-thing given shape by the Maelstrom, an assassin-priest of the Blood God, or some composite nightmare assembled from all three is a matter for those with the luck to survive their curiosity. Its voice emerges through multiple channels at once, sometimes as a judicial monotone, sometimes as a drowning man’s laugh, sometimes as what sounds like Huron’s own displeasure rendered in red static.

Its purpose is larger than murder. Kaelen’s death must instruct. His followers must understand that freedom is fiction. The world he stole must either be dragged into the Maelstrom’s orbit of terror or ruined so completely that no future captain mistakes desertion for destiny. And so the Warrant comes not as mere killer, but as a warlord, garbed in the raiment of command and accompanied by a host of the Maelstrom. Daemons, Chaos Space Marines, and red-handed zealots march in its wake, slaved to its whim or eager for the spoils of a fallen Imperial world.

For all its dread authority, there is a brazen hunger in the Warrant’s actions. It gathers skulls not merely for the gods, but as petitions. It takes heads as evidence. Every oathbreaker slain, every deserter butchered is offered upwards: to the Blood God, to the Maelstrom, to Huron Blackheart, or perhaps only to the empty place where their approval should be. Some suspect that this fanatical entity has neither met nor been sanctioned by the Tyrant at all, though they are careful never to let such whispers reach the Warrant or its followers. Such distinctions matter little to its victims. Whether servant, pretender, or masterless revenant, the Warrant lives to enforce one irresistible truth: no oath to Huron Blackheart is ever broken cleanly. 

Commander Orestes Morn

Orestes Morn has never needed to raise his voice in prayer. He believes that the God-Emperor hears discipline.

That, at least, is what those who serve under him assert. Morn is not theatrical in his devotion. He does not weep before icons, thunder scripture from balconies, or decorate every order with pious excess. His faith is colder, harder, and more dangerous: an absolute internal architecture by which the universe remains bearable. The God-Emperor endures. Humanity obeys. Treachery is punished. Sacrifice has meaning. The dead are accounted for. The chain of command is as unyielding as auramite.

To see Ferrum’s Wake as it now stands is, for Morn, to witness heresy of the highest order. Anarchy, corruption, and chaos, garbed in the false promise of freedom.

He approaches at the head of an Imperial reclamation force bearing soldiers, ships, priests, Astropathic relays, Adeptus Mechanicus envoys, the bureaucratic machinery of restored allegiance, and the essential simplicity of Orders of Execution. He comes as the return of law. He comes as the hand that steadies the drowning. 

Morn’s own faith has endured because it has never truly been asked to bend. His certainty is immense. The God-Emperor’s will must be coherent. Obedience must matter. Loyalty must be answered. Ferrum’s Wake threatens the certainty of the galaxy. Its people, if they can be called such, have committed the gravest of sins. But this world of iron can be returned to the Emperor’s grace. Across the hundreds of ships of his reclamation fleet, more than a million devout citizens of the Imperium wait at rest. They wait in prayer. 

They stand ready to replace those who traded the God-Emperor’s love for the lie of freedom.

Mara Venn, Reluctant Saint

Mara Venn was born beneath Ferrum’s Wake in a district where children learned three rules before numbers: do not trust clean water, do not sleep near vents that hum, and do not speak loudly when the machines stop.

She was not raised to be a soldier or a saint. The God-Emperor had other plans.

Before Kaelen Voss came, Mara’s people belonged to quotas, guild overseers, ration clerks, enforcer sweeps, sump debt, and the slow arithmetic of underhive survival. With the arrival of the Free Captain, they belonged to whoever could keep the oxygen shrines running and the guns loaded. Liberation changed the names on the boots. It did not keep them off anyone’s throat for long.

Mara became important by accident, which is the only way she would have tolerated it. She knew ductways others had forgotten. She could bargain with gangers, lie to warlords, steal from armouries, restart dead lumen grids, and talk frightened people into moving when staying still felt safer. She made bad deals and better escapes. She lost friends. She made bombs out of devotional fixtures. She laughed at the wrong moments and cried where no one could see.

Then the impossible began accumulating around her.

A hab-stack collapsed seconds after she pulled a refugee column through the wrong door. A corrupted servitor pack froze at the sound of a hymn she did not remember learning. A sniper round struck the aquila charm at her throat and left only a burn.

Crude graffiti of her haloed visage began terrorising her from the walls of the underhive.

Some call her a living saint of the God-Emperor. Mara herself says saints do not steal medicine at knifepoint or shoot men in the back while they reload. Yet still they come: loyal soldiers cut off from command, broken priests, repentant rebels, and every desperate soul still praying the God-Emperor will send angels to save them.

Mara is not trying to save Ferrum’s Wake. Mara knows its doom was brought by just such an angel.

But even an unwelcome burden can spark a glimmer of heroism. Mara does want to save her people. Deep in her heart, she shares their faint hope in the God-Emperor’s salvation. If only there weren’t quite so many to save.

Yesterday, we took a look at how grudge marks work for the Khazalite Holds. Today, we’re learning about their other main battle trait – Ancestral Vows.

The Khazalite Holds place their faith in several Ancestor Gods, be it Valaya – warrior goddess, and stoic defender of hearth and hold – or their indomitable death god Gazul. So strong is their belief that they can invoke some of the powers of the gods in battle – there are five potent Ancestral Vows to pick from, but each can only be used once per game.*

The effects themselves are profound. We Honour Valaya is a powerful one-time ability that heals units and dishes out damage in equal measure, and it gets even stronger when invoked on Valayan Guardians.

BATTLE TRAITS

Once Per Battle (Army), Any Hero Phase

WE HONOUR VALAYA!

These duardin ask Valaya for the strength to strike down a foe and to stand resolute in the face of adversity.

Declare: Pick up to 3 friendly DUARDIN KHAZALITE HOLDS units in combat to be blessed by Valaya. Then, for each unit blessed by Valaya this turn, pick an enemy unit in combat with it to be its target.

Effect: Roll a D3 for each unit blessed by Valaya this turn. If that unit is VALAYAN, use a value of 3 instead. Inflict an amount of mortal damage on its target equal to the roll. Then, you can pick 1 of the following:

  • Heal (X) the unit blessed by Valaya, where X is equal to the value of the roll.

  • Return a number of slain models to the unit blessed by Valaya with a combined Health characteristic of up to the value of the roll.

You cannot use any other ANCESTRAL VOW abilities for the rest of the battle round.

KEYWORDS: ANCESTRAL VOW

The fallen Slayer god Grimnir still gets respect from the Khazalites – doubly so now that the Fyreslayers have moved in to escape their overrun magmaholds. His own Ancestral Vow, Grimnir’s Wrath Will Burn Bright!, is a brutal boost to your chosen units’ fighting prowess, and can turn the tide of a hard-fought battle in moments.

BATTLE TRAITS

Once Per Battle (Army), Any Hero Phase

Roaring dedications to Grimnir, these warriors throw themselves into battle, their god’s fury coursing like magmalt ale through their veins.

Effect: For the rest of the battle round:

You cannot use any other ANCESTRAL VOW abilities for the rest of the battle round.

  • Inghilde, our Light in the Darkness – Use hidden tunnels to quickly traverse the battlefield.

  • By Grungni, Stand Firm! – Fortify your armour by remaining vigilant and not being suckered into charges.

  • Enlighten us with your Wisdom, Grombrindal – Cast spells and chant prayers more easily and resist their effects on your duardin.

As you might imagine, many of the Khazalite Holds infantry are built to make good use of these powerful bonuses – especially Inghilde’s ancestral vow.

https://www.warhammer-community.com/en-g.content_html:
Back at the Big Autumn Preview, we unveiled a brand-new faction for Warhammer Age of Sigmar – the Khazalite Holds. But what is a ‘hold’, and what secrets do they hold? Let’s find out! 

Stocky and stout-hearted duardin, the Khazalites consider themselves the truest and most honourable of this race of warriors and master crafters. The mountains are their home, great holds known as karaks, hewn into the rock. While these subterranean settlements were meant to withstand the passage of time, many lie in ruins after centuries of strife and infiltration by malign forces.

Inside a Karak

Although every Khazalite hold is unique, many share similar characteristics, regardless of the realm they are in – particularly the upper halls above ground and subterranean lower halls, which are divided into areas known as ‘deeps’.

The Upper Halls

Above the surface, but still well within the mountain, the upper levels host the living quarters of those charged with guarding the karak, and are the first – and often only – areas outsiders will see.

The Outer Gate

Hewn into the side of the mountain and flanked by statues of the ancestors, the Outer Gate is the first marker of the karak. Its mighty and striking facade hints at the scale of what is behind – and beneath – it and, as with everything of duardin construction, is built with incredible skill and of the finest materials by master craftsmen.

The Oathkeeper Battery

Protecting the Outer Gate are concealed batteries of cannons and great defences manned by Clangunners, designed to deter would-be attackers from attempting to force entry through the runic archways which mark the entry to the karak proper. Additional sentinel points are often found cut into the highest peaks of the mountain, from which any approaching foes can be spotted.

Beyond the threshold, the upper halls are usually made up of massive thronghalls – barracks for the garrison of the upper levels of the karak. Within these great spaces are brewhalls, feasting chambers, and a wanderer’s hearth by which duardin and their allies who seek respite or shelter can be warmly welcomed.

The Deeps

The lower halls, or ‘deeps’, contain the main armouries, as well as the hearths and the royal throne room. They are a hive of industry as well as remembrance. 

The Resonance Chamber

Everything in the realms, down to the matter that makes up the land, has a vibrational frequency, which the Khazalites have managed to harness. Indeed, the Khazalites believe they can ‘hear’ stone and heed the wisdom from within it. This affinity with sound led the Khazalites to build great resonance chambers, filled with gongs and horns, the sounds of which echo from the ancestor statues.

The Hall of Remembrance

Most important of all to the Khazalites is remembrance. The ancient pantheon of Ancestor Gods are revered in great ceremony – their names and deeds uttered in the hope that they will grant strength, courage, or wisdom to the current and future generations. These acts of remembrance are carried out in great halls and chambers, where the stone echoes with the sounds of these solemn rites – for to be forgotten is the worst fate of all to these duardin. 

The Forge

The pounding heart of the karak is the great forge, where duardin toil endlessly to master their craft, while vast underground farms allow each hold to be self-sufficient, and gem mines satisfy the Khazalite need to delve and explore.

The Khazalite Holds Army Set, which includes a full Spearhead and the battletome, will be available to pre-order soon, but in the meantime, you can brush up on your duardin lore in Grombrindal: Ancestor’s Burden by Chris Thursten and Gotrek and Maleneth: The Omnibus, featuring tales by Darius Hinks and Robbie MacNiven.*


* Both titles are also available as eBooks via the Black Library app.

The Legio Custodes are well known for their shining golden armour, but they’ve been shown wearing other colour schemes throughout the Age of Darkness. 

Today, we’re looking at some of the variants used during the Horus Heresy to inspire you to try something new.

The livery most associated with the demi-godlike warriors of the Legio Custodes has, since the Legio’s inception in the depths of Terran pre-history, been shining gold armour with deep red cloaks, loincloths and helmet plumes – a combination derived from the arms and devices of their master himself, the Emperor of Mankind. 

While this livery remains the standard, variants are known to exist, some of which are linked to one of the three ‘Templii Magisterium Tertia’. Each of the Templi is a loose sub-order of guardians aligned to a particular aspect of the overarching mission of the Legio Custodes, within which a Custodian might serve, sometimes for a single assignment, or in rare instances for an entire lifetime. Each of the Templii has associated with it a variation of the standard Custodes livery, and those Custodians assigned to special service with one of them are wont, on occasion, to don these unique colours in order to signal their dedication to that Templi’s specific mission.

The Templii Magisterium Tertia 

The Legio Custodes is understood to have been divided into three distinct parts, each constituted to pursue a particular element of the Emperor’s Great Work, though it was not until the fateful years of the Scouring that the full, overarching extent of this structure could be speculated upon. Revealed only to a select few beyond the Imperial Household during the wars of the Horus Heresy, and all but unknown during the Great Crusade (at least in purpose and form, if not name), the trifold Templii Magisterium Tertia’s very existence suggests a far broader mandate for the Legio Custodes than was widely understood. 

The Templi Lictoris 

Perhaps the oldest of the three Templii, the Templi Lictoris embodied, in essence, the Custodians’ role as understood by the Imperium at large – as protectors of the Emperor’s person and his companions in war. 

During the Legio Custodes’ two centuries as the speartip of the Great Crusade, it was the warriors of the Templi Lictoris who stood at the Emperor’s side as he bestrode battlefields across the galaxy and brought innumerable worlds into Compliance, and in the aftermath of Magnus’ great folly, it was they who battled desperately to prevent the terrors of the Empyrean from breaching the Imperial Dungeon. One facet of the Templii Magisterium Tertia’s concealment from the wider Imperium for such a long period likely stems from the assumption (actively promoted by the Imperial Household) that the archetype inhabited by the Templi Lictoris was representative of the Legio Custodes entire, though this could not be further from the truth. 

While Custodians undertaking duties under the specific aegis of the Templi Lictoris might wear the standard gold and red of the Legio, those with particular associations with the Lictoris and its goals might adopt the scheme shown below. This features ivory white cloaks, plumes, and panel in-fills, along with black armour with a distinct iridescent finish.

The first of the Templi Lictoris’ veiled counterparts was the Templi Prudentia, its duty being the security of the Emperor’s manifold and inscrutable plans, defending both the physical integrity of shadowed facilities across the Imperium as well as the secrecy of their contents. Their vigil safeguarded vaults laden with the weapons of Old Night, laboratories tasked with goals beyond comprehension, and prisons which entombed the Imperium’s most monstrous foes, and when the Emperor demanded some forbidden technology cloistered beyond the Imperium’s frontiers brought to Him, it was the warriors of the Templi Prudentia which saw it recovered. In the years of the Horus Heresy, both distant garrisons of the Templi Prudentia and fleets dispatched from Sol endeavoured to withhold such artefacts from the Traitors’ grasp, and at the fateful Siege of Terra, the Templi Prudentia is believed to have employed several nightmarish weapons once sequestered within their care against the Warmaster’s armies.

The Templi Veritas 

The final division of the Templii Magisterium Tertia is that whose role was shielded most ardently from those outside of the Imperial Household, for its implications and history were fell indeed. Its remit was that of the executioner: the eradication of any element held unworthy by the Emperor, be it due to betrayal or simple obsolescence, such that not even its memory endured. It is believed to have been the Custodians of this ‘Templi Veritas’ which enacted the cull of the Thunder Warriors at Mount Ararat, and who saw to the disposal of those deemed tainted in the final days of the second Rangdan campaign, alongside countless other grim duties all but erased from memory. 

During and following the Horus Heresy, they were the most bellicose of the Legio Custodes, and where their conquests were unable to scour all trace of their foe from existence, they were instead conducted with symbolic precision, inflicting pinpoint destruction upon worlds such as Chemos and Arachnus as harrowing displays of the Emperor’s judgement. Within this era, the number of Custodians active as part of the Templi Veritas defied all outside understanding of the Legio Custodes’ strength, especially in light of the bloody Webway conflict, leading some to suppose that, in secret, the Templi Veritas had been in the midst of shadowed preparations for some purge yet to come when the Horus Heresy erupted.

Let’s start with the new Champion pack. The Space Wolves send one of their best with an incredible new armour set based on the Wolf Guard Battle Leader, complete with a round Fenrisian storm shield so you can use it with the Bulwark class. 

This modified MkX Tacticus suit is covered in furs and fangs befitting one of the Chapter’s most storied veterans.

But wait, what’s that he’s holding up there? From today, players can bash xenos skulls in and sunder Rubric power armour with a mighty one-handed thunder hammer! This brutal weapon is faster than the two-handed variant and can charge up to deal rippling area-of-effect blows, making it a great option for all kinds of foes.

Players using the Tactical, Assault, Bulwark, and Techmarines classes can all take the one-handed thunder hammer into battle, and there’s even a powerful Heroic version – the Power Maul.

These come alongside top-end additions for the power axe, auto bolt rifle, and five new cosmetic items bought with Accolades, including a fancy shoulderpad for the Black Templars and an Iron Halo.

The Tactical class is getting a top-to-bottom rework in this patch, renovating large swathes of its skill tree to offer more varied and interesting build options. It will also be getting access to the one-handed thunder hammer, the power axe, and the power sword, though with any of these powerful melee options equipped, you’ll lose access to your primary weapon.

So what if you want to take a bolt rifle and a power axe? There’s actually a Signature Perk for that – replacing the old Signal Jammer, you’ll now be able to choose an option that lets you take the regular, humble bolt rifle in your secondary weapon slot, with progression shared with its normal primary slot version. Tactical specialists really are the most versatile Space Marines in the squad.

If you’re looking for more of a challenge to test out the new skills, or simply enjoy running through Operations as close to the wire as possible, try out the new Crucible mode to earn Crucible XP. By talking to the Company Chaplain on board the battle barge you can activate Penances – personal debuffs that make your run harder – and completing missions with them active will put you on track to earning a set of Lamenters armour pieces.

Alongside the Space Wolves Champion Pack, the mysterious Exorcists Chapter also gets a Cosmetic Pack added to the Season Pass. This set of stylised armour pieces includes one Helmet, two Left and Right Pauldrons, two Left and Right Gauntlets, and one Breastplate from everyone’s favourite daemon-hunting Successor Chapter, covered in purity seals and arcane script.  The Space Wolves Champion pack and Exorcists Chapter Pack are available to buy individually and also as part of Season Pass 3, whilst everything else included in the update is free. 

Fancy getting a bit traitorous? A new spin on the wave-based Siege mode lets you step into the boots of a Chaos Space Marine to slaughter Tyranids, Imperial Guardsmen, and even loyalist Space Marines as you fight for dominion over Avarax. The new mode will initially include two sectors, with a third planned for a later release.

On top of all of this, we’ve still got room for a few more free additions. Heroic weapon variants of the power axe, one-handed thunder hammer, and auto bolt rifle will be added to the armoury, along with five new armour pieces and an expansion of the wargear sharing system. A third slot will open up to be used with capes, tabards, and iron halos, while some new items for Vanguard, Heavy, and Assault classes can be unlocked with new Ordeals.

This is only the first big update coming over the next 12 months, and the Year 3 battle plan is stacked with enough new content to fill a battle barge, from new weapons and new operations to an entirely new class – the Apothecary! Check out our first look at the schedule.

And that just about covers it! Head into Warhammer 40,000: Space Marine 2 now to try out the new update, and get yourself prepared for Year 3.

We’ve shown the Adeptus Custodes’ new army rules and detachments, so today we’re looking at some detachment combinations to help you hit the ground running when the codex drops.

We’ve put together a couple of options for detachment combos, and give some advice on units you could use to make the biggest impact on the battlefield.

Even Harder to Kill

  • Shadowkeepers (1 Detachment Point)

  • Honoured Companions (1 Detachment Point)

  • Null Maiden Vigil (1 Detachment Point)

This detachment combination would be useful with Custodian Guard Sodality and Custodian Wardens forming the backbone of your army, led by Shield-Captains and supported by units of Witchseeker Squads.

The Custodian Wardens are some of the hardest nuts to crack in the new Codex, their Living Fortress ability giving attacks against them -1 AP. When on an objective, they (and other Adeptus Custodes units) will benefit from attacks against them having -1 to wound rolls if the attack’s Strength is higher than their Toughness, thanks to the Wardens of the Dark Cells detachment rule. Equip them with castellan axes to counter some of the most elite enemies in the galaxy and, with support from the Companion’s Watch detachment rule and the Avenge the Fallen stratagem,* you’ll be throwing out upwards of 15 attacks at 10 S, -2 AP, 4 D, re-rolling wound rolls of 1. 

DETACHMENT RULES

HONOURED COMPANIONS

COMPANION’S WATCH

Among the Companions and the Sentinel Guard, vigilance is the most crucial of attributes.

While a friendly TRUSTED SENTINEL unit is within range of an objective, that unit’s attacks can re-roll wound rolls of 1.

More excitingly, if you don’t end up needing to use the Avenge the Fallen stratagem, the Emperor’s Domain stratagem in your opponent’s Fight phase allows you to make a consolidation move out of combat provided you end that move on an objective. As this happens after your opponent has already consolidated, you’ll be primed and ready to shoot and charge your foes once again in your own turn. An excellent use of 1CP.

AVENGE THE FALLEN (1CP)

HONOURED COMPANIONS STRATAGEM

The loss of a single Custodian is commemorated by the tolling of the Bell of Lost Souls on Terra, and by their comrades’ bloody vengeance on the battlefield

WHEN: Fight phase, when a friendly TRUSTED SENTINEL unit that is below starting strength is selected to fight.

TARGET: That TRUSTED SENTINEL unit. 

EFFECT: Your unit’s melee attacks (excluding those made by CHARACTER models) have +2 A.

EMPEROR’S DOMAIN (1CP)

HONOURED COMPANIONS STRATAGEM

There are those territories that must remain in the hands of the Imperium and be free of foes, regardless of the cost. 

WHEN: Fight phase, when a friendly TRUSTED SENTINEL unit is selected to make a consolidation move.

TARGET: That TRUSTED SENTINEL unit. 

EFFECT: You can select the objective consolidation mode for that consolidation move, regardless of that consolidation move’s Before Moving restrictions.

This means your unit can move out of engagement range with enemy units, provided it meets the conditions of the objective consolidation mode.

Meanwhile your Custodian Guard Sodality will be better used as a crowbar to pry enemies from objectives, using their Impenetrable Defence ability to gain Sustained Hits 1 against anything that isn’t a Monster or Vehicle.

The Shield-Captains could be attached to either of these units, as they will allow you to either use two different ka’tah abilities in the same battle round, or one in your and your opponent’s turns, allowing your units to exercise total flexibility in all situations.

DETACHMENT RULES

NULL MAIDEN VIGIL

SILENT SISTERHOOD

The Null Maidens of the Silent Sisterhood bring with them the nightmare pall of their collective null aura, afflicting their opponents with a creeping sense of dread.

  • When mustering your army, you can select a friendly ANATHEMA PSYKANA CHARACTER model to be your WARLORD.

  • Friendly PROSECUTOR SQUAD units have BATTLELINE.

  • Friendly ANATHEMA PSYKANA units have the following ability:

Creeping Dread (Aura): In the Battle-shock step of your opponent’s Command phase, each enemy unit within 12" of this unit that is a PSYKER unit/below starting strength makes a battle-shock roll, with -1 to that battle-shock roll.

In the case of some stubborn enemy units on objectives or problematic stratagem potentials, the Witchseekers can battle-shock your opponent’s units either by shooting them in your turn or using the Creeping Dread ability from the Null Maiden Vigil detachment to deny those more resilient units a chance to hold objectives or use stratagems.

Hyper-elite Fighting Machines

  • Dread Host (1 Detachment Point)

  • Lions of the Emperor (1 Detachment Point)

  • Might of the Moritoi (1 Detachment Point)

This combination is all about maximising your melee superiority, through the mobility of Terminators backed up by Dreadnoughts.

Through the Lions of the Emperor detachment rule, your Terminator units have total board control, by being able to return to strategic reserves, allowing them to reappear later wherever the need is most dire.** This is especially potent if you include a variety of Terminator units in your army, as each excels against specific targets. 

DETACHMENT RULES
LIONS OF THE EMPEROR

ON GILDED WINGS

Terminator sodalities are swept up by golden drop craft, ready to be deployed once more as battle demands.

At the end of your opponent’s Fight phase, if a friendly ADEPTUS CUSTODES TERMINATOR unit is unengaged, you can place that unit in strategic reserves.

Allarus Custodians are excellent at bringing down even the most towering of foes, Aquilon Terminators with solarite power gauntlets want to break apart elite infantry and light vehicles, and those with solarite power talons want to find the nearest horde and wipe it out. Their manoeuvrability means you can always apply the correct tool in the right location, and makes it difficult for your opponent to react to your next move.

Dread Host allows your Terminator units to have dramatically improved chances of making a charge after arriving from strategic reserves, by giving you a crucial charge re-roll. You can put the odds further in your favour by using the Fury of the Emperor stratagem to get +2 to that charge roll, while still re-rolling if required.

A Telemon Heavy Dreadnought or two make an already terrifying army even scarier for your opponent. They now sport a near Primarch-level statline, and one of these might just be your best answer to fighting against another Custodes army.***

One of these units can be given the Memento Moritoi upgrade, which gives your unit +1 A, S, and D to its melee attacks. Dual caestus fists are now A8 , S15, and D5. That’s a flattened Custodian Guard Sodality every time you attack, and you’ll be re-rolling the wound roll to ensure you push the pain through.

These are just some suggestions to get you battling the enemies of the Golden Throne as quickly as possible, but we look forward to seeing what you come up with too when the new Codex goes up for pre-order on Saturday.

* Should any of your Wardens have fallen.
** Sometimes referred to as being “uppy downy”.
*** Here are some other things your vaunted Custodes need to look out for.
